## Part 6 · Put the workflow together

Two projects take a new public-data question from inputs to a figure, a regression table and interpretation notes. Complete Parts 0–5 first. Plan for 60–90 minutes per project, split across sessions as needed. The second gives less step-by-step guidance.

### 6.1 Fertility and income

In 2019, did higher-income economies have lower total fertility rates? The World Bank snapshot retains 217 economies, with 211 complete income/fertility pairs. This first project provides more explicit steps.

### 6.2 Internet use and urbanization

Were more urbanized economies also more connected in 2019? The World Bank snapshot retains 217 economies, with 189 complete internet-use/urban-share pairs. This second project asks you to plan more of the analysis yourself.

## How to work

1. Open the starter in Colab or download it and upload your own copy. Each notebook includes the prepared package and frozen-data setup; no repository credentials or live-data API key are needed to run that copy.
2. Read the question, units and source notes. Run the supplied setup and input checks. The cells marked **TODO** are deliberately incomplete: running the starter alone does not solve the project.
3. Write the sample, chart, estimation and export steps. Keep original inputs, count missing values and check unique keys. Give each result its units and observation year.
4. Explain the result in words before comparing with the complete solution. A different defensible specification can answer a different question; do not change code merely to match an expected sign or p-value.
5. Restart and run the notebook from the top. Verify the exported numbers against the fitted results and keep source/interpretation notes with the figure and table.

## Sources and limits

These are **2019 observations in snapshots retrieved 2026-11-11**, not current statistics. World Bank geography includes countries and territories. Each economy receives equal weight; neither project estimates the average person's behaviour. The [data dictionary and provenance](https://github.com/ningzhanglab/Python-for-Beginners/blob/main/data/README.md) records raw API requests, hashes, definitions, transformations, missingness and source licenses.

The indicator metadata explicitly identifies CC BY 4.0 with the World Bank's additional terms. Credit the World Bank and original providers: national/OECD/World Bank accounts and UN/national/Eurostat fertility sources in 6.1; the International Telecommunication Union and UN Population Division in 6.2. The course's original presentation remains unlicensed pending the owner's decision.

Both projects use OLS with explicit HC1 uncertainty and compare the same sample across specifications. They do not identify causal effects of income or urbanization. Missingness, different national definitions, source-estimate uncertainty and cross-economy dependence remain limitations. The complete solution is a transparent teaching analysis, not a policy recommendation.

Use [regression interpretation](../lessons/04-regression/02-correlation-ols.ipynb), [uncertainty choices](../lessons/04-regression/04-robust-clustered.ipynb), [reproducible folders](../lessons/05-workflow/02-folders-paths-scripts.ipynb) and the [reference pages](../reference/index.qmd) when you need a reminder.
